title: Quick Sort
description: Learn how **Quick Sort** uses **pivot partitioning** and Divide and Conquer recursion to efficiently organize data through recursive partition reduction.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
**Quick Sort** is a highly efficient sorting algorithm based on the **Divide and Conquer strategy**.

*   It was developed by British computer scientist Tony Hoare in 1959.
*   Instead of repeatedly swapping adjacent elements like Bubble Sort, Quick Sort selects a special element called the **pivot**.
*   It partitions the array around the pivot, and **recursively sorts** the left and right partitions.

Think of it like organizing a bookshelf by genre:
1.  You pick a pivot genre like Science Fiction.
2.  You put all Science Fiction books together in the middle.
3.  You place all books that come before Science Fiction alphabetically on the left, and all books that come after on the right.
4.  Then you **repeat the process** on the left section and right section independently.

Quick Sort is often the **fastest comparison-based sort in practice** for random data.
*   It works **in-place** with minimal memory allocation.
*   Partitioning has **good cache locality** because it accesses memory sequentially.
*   The constant factors are lower than Merge Sort.

C++ standard library uses Introsort which is Quick Sort with a fallback.
Java uses Dual-Pivot Quick Sort for sorting primitives.
Many programming languages use Quick Sort or its variants as their **default sorting algorithm** for primitive data types.

sections.title: Why Quick Sort Matters
sections.content:
Sorting is one of the most common operations in computing.

Databases, search engines, analytics systems, recommendation systems, and AI pipelines **constantly sort enormous amounts of data**.
The choice of sorting algorithm can dramatically impact system performance.

For n equals 1 million random elements:
*   **Bubble Sort** takes about 500 billion operations which could take days.
*   **Merge Sort** takes about 20 million operations plus O(n) memory.
*   **Quick Sort** takes about 20 million operations plus O(log n) stack space and is **often faster than Merge Sort in practice**.

Although Merge Sort guarantees stable O(n log n) performance, Quick Sort is often faster in real-world systems because:
1.  **Partitioning is efficient**.
2.  **Memory overhead is smaller**.
3.  **Cache performance is better**.

Quick Sort has lower constant factors and fewer data movements than Merge Sort.

For random data of size 10 million, Quick Sort typically takes about 2 to 3 seconds while Merge Sort takes about 4 to 5 seconds due to memory allocation.
This is why Quick Sort is the **default choice for general-purpose sorting** in many systems.
bullets: Quick Sort performs **extremely fast on average**.
Modern systems commonly use **Quick Sort variants**.

sections.title: Core Idea of Quick Sort
sections.content:
Quick Sort works through **partitioning**. This is the heart of the algorithm.

The algorithm follows these core steps:
1.  It selects a **pivot element**.
2.  It moves **smaller elements** to the left side.
3.  It moves **larger elements** to the right side.
4.  It **recursively sorts** both partitions.

After partitioning, the pivot reaches its **correct sorted position**.
Recursive partitioning repeatedly reduces disorder until the entire array becomes sorted.

This is classic **Divide and Conquer**:
*   The **divide step** is partitioning around the pivot.
*   The **conquer step** is recursively sorting the left and right partitions.
*   The **combine step** is trivial because the pivot is already in place.

For example, start with `[8, 3, 5, 1, 7]`. Choose pivot `7`.
After partitioning, the array becomes `[3, 5, 1, 7, 8]`. The pivot `7` is now in its **final position**.
Then recursively sort `[3, 5, 1]` and `[8]`. Continue until fully sorted.

Unlike Merge Sort which divides first then sorts during merge, Quick Sort **sorts during partition** then recursively processes smaller subproblems.
The pivot ends up in its correct position after each partition, so **each recursive call places one more element correctly**.

sections.title: Understanding the Pivot
sections.content:
The pivot is the central element used to partition the array.
**Pivot selection significantly impacts Quick Sort's performance**.

*   A **good pivot** creates balanced partitions with sizes roughly n/2 each, leading to **O(n log n)** performance.
*   A **bad pivot** creates unbalanced partitions like 1 element on one side and n-1 on the other, leading to **O(n squared)** performance.

Common pivot selection strategies include:
1.  **First or last element:** Simple but terrible for already sorted arrays, causing O(n squared).
2.  **Random element:** Makes worst-case O(n squared) extremely unlikely, with probability approaching zero.
3.  **Median of three:** Chooses the median of the first, middle, and last elements, providing excellent pivot quality.

For example, with array `[8, 3, 5, 1, 7]` and pivot `7`, the goal is to place values smaller than 7 on the left and values larger than 7 on the right.
After partitioning, 7 ends up at index 3: `[3, 5, 1, 7, 8]`. The pivot acts as a **dividing boundary**.

Choosing a bad pivot like the smallest or largest element creates a skewed recursion tree with depth O(n) instead of O(log n).
For n equals 1 million, balanced depth is about 20 while skewed depth is 1 million, which would cause stack overflow.
This is why **pivot selection is critical**.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Partition Example
sections.content:
Suppose we sort the array `[8, 3, 5, 1, 7]` using **pivot 7**.

The algorithm compares every element with the pivot:
*   Values 3, 5, and 1 are **smaller** than 7, while 8 is **larger**.
*   After partitioning, the array becomes `[3, 5, 1, 7, 8]`.
*   Notice that 7 is now in its **final sorted position** at index 3.

The algorithm then recursively sorts the left partition `[3, 5, 1]` and the right partition `[8]`.
1.  For the left partition, choose **pivot 1**. Values 3 and 5 are larger, so after partitioning we get `[1, 3, 5]`.
2.  For `[3, 5]`, choose **pivot 5** to get `[3, 5]`.
3.  The right partition `[8]` is **already sorted**.

Here is the complete trace:
*   Start with `[8, 3, 5, 1, 7]`.
*   Partition with pivot 7 gives `[3, 5, 1, 7, 8]`.
*   Recursively sort left `[3, 5, 1]`. Partition with pivot 1 gives `[1, 3, 5]`.
*   Recursively sort `[3, 5]`. Partition with pivot 5 gives `[3, 5]`.
*   **Final result is `[1, 3, 5, 7, 8]`**.

In the **Lomuto partition scheme**, the algorithm works **in-place** within the original array.
It uses a pointer `i` to track the boundary of smaller elements.
For each element, if it is less than the pivot, it is swapped into the left section. At the end, the pivot is swapped into its correct position.

sections.title: Understanding Recursive Partitioning
sections.content:
Quick Sort repeatedly partitions smaller subarrays. This recursive decomposition is what makes Quick Sort a **Divide and Conquer algorithm**.

With a **good pivot**, the recursion tree is balanced:
*   Level 0 has n elements.
*   Level 1 has n/2 and n/2.
*   Level 2 has n/4, n/4, n/4, n/4.
*   The depth is **log base 2 of n**.

With a **bad pivot**, the recursion tree is skewed:
*   Level 0 has n elements.
*   Level 1 has 0 and n-1.
*   Level 2 has 0 and n-2.
*   The depth is **n**.

For n equals 1 billion, balanced depth is about 30, which is safe.
Skewed depth is 1 billion, which would cause stack overflow.
This is why **pivot selection is critical**. Random pivot or median-of-three guarantees reasonable balance.

Quick Sort exemplifies **Divide and Conquer**:
1.  **Divide step:** Partitions the array around the pivot.
2.  **Conquer step:** Recursively sorts the left and right partitions.
3.  **Combine step:** Trivial because the pivot is already in place and partitions are sorted independently.

Each recursive step **reduces disorder further** until the array becomes fully sorted.

sections.title: Why Quick Sort Is Fast
sections.content:
Quick Sort becomes efficient because partitioning **rapidly reduces problem size** while operating **in-place with good cache locality**.
Balanced partitions create recursive trees similar to repeatedly dividing n into n/2, then n/4, then n/8.

Even though both Quick Sort and Merge Sort are O(n log n) in expectation, Quick Sort often **outperforms Merge Sort in practice** for several reasons:
*   Quick Sort **sorts in-place** using O(log n) stack space, while Merge Sort requires O(n) auxiliary arrays with memory allocation and copying overhead.
*   Quick Sort's partition phase scans sequentially through the array, which is **cache-friendly**.
*   Quick Sort moves elements **only during partitioning**, while Merge Sort moves every element during each merge level.

For random data of size 10 million, Quick Sort typically takes about 2 to 3 seconds.
Merge Sort takes about 4 to 5 seconds due to memory allocation. Bubble Sort would take weeks.

However, Quick Sort is **not always fast**:
1.  Already sorted data with first or last pivot causes **O(n squared)** behavior.
2.  Data with many equal elements can also cause problems unless optimized.
3.  When stable sorting is required, Quick Sort is not suitable because it is **not stable**.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content:
Quick Sort implementations usually rely on **recursive partitioning and pivot-based decomposition**.

*   The **simple version** creates new left and right arrays for each partition. This is easy to understand but uses O(n log n) extra space.
*   The **in-place version** sorts within the original array using O(log n) stack space.

In the simple version:
1.  The **base case** is when the array length is less than or equal to 1, in which case it returns the array.
2.  Otherwise, it chooses a pivot, typically the **last element**.
3.  It creates left and right lists, placing elements smaller than the pivot into left and elements greater than or equal into right.
4.  Then it **recursively sorts left and right** and returns left plus pivot plus right.

The in-place version uses the **Lomuto partition scheme**:
*   It chooses the last element as pivot.
*   It uses a pointer `i` to track the boundary of elements less than the pivot.
*   It iterates `j` from low to high minus 1.
*   If `arr[j]` is less than or equal to the pivot, it swaps `arr[i]` and `arr[j]` and increments `i`.
*   After the loop, it swaps the pivot into position `i`.
*   Then it recursively calls itself on the left and right partitions.

**Random pivot selection avoids worst-case behavior**. Median-of-three pivot selection is even better for production code.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
Quick Sort achieves **O(n log n) average-case complexity** because balanced partitions repeatedly reduce the problem size.

*   The **best case** occurs when the pivot always partitions the array into two equal halves.
*   The recurrence is T(n) = 2T(n/2) plus O(n), which solves to **O(n log n)**.

However, **worst-case performance can become O(n squared)** when partitions become extremely unbalanced.
*   If the pivot always selects the smallest or largest element, the recurrence becomes T(n) = T(n-1) plus O(n), which solves to **O(n squared)**.
*   This happens with already sorted data when using first or last element pivot.

For n equals 1 million:
1.  **Balanced Quick Sort** takes about 20 million comparisons.
2.  **Skewed Quick Sort** takes about 500 billion comparisons, which is **25,000 times slower**.
3.  For sorted data with last element pivot, Quick Sort degrades to **O(n squared)**.

Many Quick Sort implementations also achieve **good memory efficiency** because they sort in-place.
*   The iterative in-place version uses **O(log n) stack space** on average.
*   The worst-case stack space is O(n) if partitions are skewed, which can cause stack overflow.
*   To avoid this, production implementations use **random pivot** or **median-of-three** and may switch to Heap Sort for deep recursion, which is called **Introsort**.

sections.title: Why Worst-Case O(n^2) Happens
sections.content:
Worst-case performance occurs when **partitioning repeatedly produces highly uneven sections**.

Suppose the array is already sorted as `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` and the algorithm always chooses the **last element as the pivot**.
Each partition creates a left partition of size n-1 and a right partition of size 0:
1.  **Partition 1** with pivot 5 gives left `[1, 2, 3, 4]` and right `[]`.
2.  **Partition 2** with pivot 4 gives left `[1, 2, 3]` and right `[]`.
3.  **Partition 3** with pivot 3 gives left `[1, 2]` and right `[]`.
4.  **Partition 4** with pivot 2 gives left `[1]` and right `[]`.

This creates a **skewed recursion tree with depth n**.

The comparison count becomes (n-1) plus (n-2) plus (n-3) plus ... plus 1, which equals n times n-1 divided by 2, which is **O(n squared)**.
For n equals 1 million, this is about 500 billion comparisons.

To avoid worst case, **use random pivot selection**.
*   This makes worst-case extremely unlikely.
*   The probability of consistently picking bad pivots is 1 over n factorial, which is practically zero for large n.
*   **Median-of-three pivot selection** also guarantees a moderate pivot.
*   **Introsort** switches to Heap Sort if recursion depth exceeds log n, guaranteeing O(n log n) even with bad pivots.

sections.title: Quick Sort vs Merge Sort
sections.content:
Quick Sort uses partitioning, while Merge Sort uses merging.
Both algorithms commonly achieve O(n log n) average performance, but Quick Sort **often performs faster in practice** because memory overhead is lower and cache behavior is better.

For random data of size 1 million:
*   **Quick Sort** typically takes about 0.3 to 0.5 seconds in-place.
*   **Merge Sort** takes about 0.5 to 0.8 seconds due to memory allocation and copying.
*   Quick Sort is **often 1.5 to 2 times faster**.

However, Merge Sort provides **stable sorting** and guaranteed worst-case O(n log n) behavior, while Quick Sort may degrade to O(n squared) with poor pivot selection.

Merge Sort is better when:
1.  Stability is required.
2.  Worst-case performance must be guaranteed for real-time systems.
3.  Data is already sorted or reverse-sorted.
4.  Sorting linked lists.
5.  External sorting is needed when data is too large for memory.

Language Defaults:
*   **C++ std::sort** uses Introsort which is Quick Sort with a fallback to Heap Sort.
*   **Java Arrays.sort** for primitives uses Dual-Pivot Quick Sort.
*   **Java Arrays.sort** for objects uses Timsort, which is Merge Sort plus Insertion Sort.
*   **Python sort** uses Timsort because Quick Sort is not stable.

**Choose based on your specific requirements** for speed, memory, stability, and data characteristics.

sections.title: In-Place Sorting
sections.content:
Many Quick Sort implementations are considered **in-place algorithms**.
This means sorting occurs **directly within the original array** instead of requiring large auxiliary arrays.
The partition operation swaps elements within the array rather than creating new lists.

In-place Quick Sort memory usage:
*   Uses **O(log n) stack space** for recursion on average and O(n) in the worst case.
*   For n equals 10 million, in-place Quick Sort uses about 80 megabytes for the array itself plus about 240 bytes for the stack with about 20 frames times 12 bytes.
*   Merge Sort would use 80 megabytes for the original array plus 80 megabytes for temporary arrays, totaling 160 megabytes.

In-place sorting **improves memory efficiency, cache performance, and scalability** for large datasets.
The original array order is lost, but for sorting large datasets, memory efficiency often outweighs this concern.

The **Lomuto and Hoare partition schemes** both work in-place:
1.  They use two pointers to track positions and swap elements when they are on the wrong side of the pivot.
2.  At the end, the pivot is placed in its correct position.
3.  The Hoare partition scheme is more efficient but harder to understand.
4.  The examples in this lesson use the simpler Lomuto scheme.

subsections.title: Limitations
bullets: **Poor pivot selection** can severely reduce efficiency.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
Quick Sort appears in standard libraries, database systems, analytics pipelines, compiler optimization, search systems, and AI preprocessing systems.
Its **fast practical performance and low memory overhead** make it one of the most important sorting algorithms in computer science.

Standard Library Usage:
*   **C++ std::sort** uses Introsort, which is Quick Sort with a Heap Sort fallback to guarantee O(n log n).
*   **Java Arrays.sort** for primitives uses Dual-Pivot Quick Sort, which is faster than classic Quick Sort.
*   **Go sort package** uses Quick Sort with optimizations.
*   **Rust sort_unstable** uses a variant of Quick Sort.

System Applications:
*   **Database systems** use Quick Sort for in-memory sorting of intermediate results in query processing.
*   **Operating systems** use Quick Sort in various kernel sorting routines.
*   **ETL pipelines** sort large datasets for aggregation and reporting.
*   **Gaming** uses Quick Sort for leaderboards and inventory systems.

Quick Sort is the **default choice for general-purpose sorting** in many systems because it works well for most real-world data distributions.
However, it is not used when stability is required (such as in Python which uses Timsort) or when worst-case guarantees are required for real-time systems (which may use Heap Sort or Merge Sort).

subsections.title: Mistake: Confusing pivot selection with sorting itself
subsections.content:
The pivot only **partitions the array into sections**.
Recursive partitioning and repeated decomposition produce the final sorted result. Partitioning places one element, the pivot, correctly. **Recursion places all other elements correctly**.

subsections.title: Mistake: Incorrect partition boundaries
subsections.content:
Incorrect boundaries may create infinite recursion, skipped elements, or incorrect sorting behavior.
**Always exclude the pivot** from recursive calls. Use low to pivot index minus 1 for the left side and pivot index plus 1 to high for the right side.

subsections.title: Mistake: Assuming Quick Sort is always O(n log n)
subsections.content:
Poor pivot selection can produce highly unbalanced partitions and **degrade performance to O(n squared)**.
The worst case is not just theoretical. It happens in practice with sorted data when using first or last pivot. **Always use random pivot or median-of-three** in production code.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: The algorithm **partitions arrays around a pivot**.
Smaller elements **move left** of the pivot.
Larger elements **move right** of the pivot.
Poor pivot selection may **cause O(n^2) behavior**.
